opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the very practical problems you run into as soon as you let a language model rewrite code inside an evolutionary loop. If you just hand the model the whole file and say "improve this," it will happily rewrite things you never wanted touched: the evaluation harness, the function signatures the scorer depends on, the input/output format, sometimes even the scoring logic itself. Then you either get crashes or, worse, a program that looks great because it has quietly changed what's being measured.

So the first thing we do is make the mutable region explicit. In the program you mark blocks with something like an "evolve block start" and "evolve block end" comment. Everything inside those markers is fair game for the LLM, and everything outside is treated as fixed scaffolding: imports, the entry point the evaluator calls, data loading, the checks that validate the output. When we build the mutation prompt, we show the model the full context so it understands how its code will be used, but we tell it clearly that only the marked regions can change. Then, critically, we don't just trust it. When the response comes back, we splice the edits into those regions programmatically and reconstruct the file around the untouched parts. If the model tries to edit outside the markers, that edit simply doesn't land.

The second piece is how the edits are represented. We support a few modes. One is diff-based, where the model emits search-and-replace blocks: here is the exact original snippet, here is the replacement. That's very token-efficient and works well for small, local changes, but it's brittle. If the model misquotes the original text by even a whitespace character, the patch fails to apply. So we have a full-rewrite mode for the evolve block, which is more robust for larger structural changes but costs more tokens and tends to lose more of the parent's good ideas. And there's crossover-style prompting, where the model sees two parents and is asked to combine them. Mixing these, and even letting the system adapt which mode it uses, gives you a good balance between exploration and not breaking things.

The third piece is validation before evaluation. Every candidate goes through cheap checks first: does the patch apply, does the file parse, does it compile or import, does it run on a tiny input within a time limit? If any of that fails, we don't throw the attempt away silently. We can feed the error message back to the model and let it repair the patch, with a small retry budget. That reflection loop recovers a surprising fraction of candidates that would otherwise be wasted, and it's far cheaper than paying for a full evaluation on something broken.

Finally there's the reward-hacking angle. Because the evaluator lives outside the mutable region and runs in its own process, the model can't simply edit its way to a high score. We also validate outputs independently. For a packing problem, for example, we recheck that the circles are inside the boundary and don't overlap, rather than trusting whatever the program reports about itself. So the overall principle is to be very explicit about what is allowed to change, enforce that mechanically rather than through instructions alone, catch failures early and cheaply, and keep the thing that decides fitness entirely out of the model's reach.

r001.rationale: The response describes marking an “evolve block” with start and end comments, making only the code inside eligible for mutation.

r002.rationale: The response says edits outside the markers are discarded, but does not describe resampling the mutation proposal when it attempts to modify protected code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we ran into head-on with the ShinkaEvolve work, and really with any of these evolutionary code systems like AlphaEvolve or FunSearch. The core tension is that you want the LLM to be creative, to really explore the program space, but you also have a harness around that program that has to stay intact, because otherwise you're not evaluating what you think you're evaluating. If the model rewrites the scoring function or the entry point, you've lost the ground truth.

The simplest and honestly most effective thing we do is to mark up the code explicitly. You have regions that are mutable and regions that are immutable, and you communicate that to the model through comments or markers, something like "EVOLVE-BLOCK-START" and "EVOLVE-BLOCK-END". Everything outside of those blocks is the evaluation scaffolding, the I/O, the metric computation, and we just don't let the model touch it. And we don't rely on the model to respect that purely through the prompt. We actually enforce it on the parsing side, so even if the model produces a full rewrite, we only splice back in the parts that fall within the editable regions and keep the protected code as it was.

The second piece is the mutation format itself. We use a mix of operators. There's a diff-based edit where the model proposes search-and-replace patches, and that's quite surgical, which is great for small, targeted changes, but it's brittle because the search string has to match exactly, and LLMs are not always perfect at copying a block verbatim. So you need fuzzy matching and fallback logic, and you need to be willing to just discard a mutation if it doesn't apply cleanly. Then there's full rewrite, where the model rewrites the whole editable block, which is more robust in the sense that it almost always parses, but it tends to drift more. And then we have crossover-style operators where we show the model multiple parents and ask it to combine ideas. Having a portfolio of these and sampling between them makes the whole system more robust than any single one.

And then the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that the evaluator itself is a filter. A lot of mutations will just fail. They'll throw an exception, they'll time out, they'll produce something that doesn't type-check. And that's fine. You treat that as a very low fitness, you record the error trace, and critically, you feed that trace back to the model in subsequent prompts. So the model sees, "here's a program, here's how it failed," and that's actually a very useful signal for the next round. The robustness comes from the population dynamics as much as from any single mutation being correct.

One more thing I'd add is that we became quite paranoid about reward hacking. If there's any way for the program to peek at the test cases or to short-circuit the metric, a sufficiently clever model will eventually find it, not out of any malice, just because it's optimizing. So we keep the evaluation in a separate process, often sandboxed, with the test data not accessible from the program's scope. The protected regions help, but the real guarantee has to come from the isolation of the evaluation.

r001.rationale: It describes marking mutable and immutable regions in the code with comments or markers such as “EVOLVE-BLOCK-START” and “EVOLVE-BLOCK-END”.

r002.rationale: It says to enforce protected regions by splicing back only editable parts, but does not describe resampling a proposal when it attempts to modify protected code.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the part of the program that can evolve from the infrastructure that evaluates it. You give the LLM a clearly marked region to modify, and then apply its proposed change only within that region. The evaluator, the interface, and any essential scaffolding stay fixed. You don’t rely on a prompt saying, “Please don’t change this”—you enforce that boundary when you construct the candidate program.

Then you treat every mutation as untrusted: check that it parses, check that it satisfies the interface, and execute it in an isolated environment with resource limits. If it fails, you reject it and keep the parent. You can also feed the error back to the model for a repair attempt. So the LLM proposes changes, but the surrounding system decides whether those changes are valid and whether they actually improve performance.

r001.rationale: It says to give the LLM a clearly marked region to modify and apply changes only within that region.

r002.rationale: It says to reject a failed mutation and keep the parent, with an optional repair attempt. It does not describe resampling a proposal that tries to modify protected code.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the program into the part the model is allowed to mutate and the part that defines the evaluation. The evaluator, the interface, and any essential scaffolding should be protected by construction. Rather than asking the model to rewrite the entire file and hoping it preserves those pieces, have it return a replacement for a specific function or an editable block, then insert that into a fixed template.

You then need a validation loop: does the result parse, does it preserve the required interface, and can it actually execute under the resource limits? If it fails, you can feed the error back to the model for repair or reject the mutation. The important distinction is that prompting encourages the model to respect the constraints; the surrounding system enforces them.

r001.rationale: It proposes returning a replacement for a specific function or editable block and inserting it into a fixed template, but does not describe markers in program text that designate eligible regions.

r002.rationale: It says to repair or reject a failed mutation, but does not describe resampling when a proposal attempts to modify protected code.
